questions.stem: A user keeps pressing a thermostat to 30° to heat the room faster. What does this show?
options: An inaccurate mental model of how the thermostat works
A gulf of evaluation caused by missing feedback
questions.explanation: The user believes a higher setting heats faster, like a tap; a thermostat only switches on or off. That is an inaccurate mental model, which users use to predict what will happen (Slide 4).
questions.hint: What does the user believe is going on inside the device?
questions.workedExample: Worked example (Slide 4): someone presses the lift call button repeatedly, believing more presses bring the lift sooner. Their mental model is that the button is a 'hurry' control, which it is not.

questions.stem: Why do menus usually beat typed commands for new users?
options: Recognising an option is easier than recalling a command
questions.explanation: Recognition is easier than recall, so showing options helps (Slide 3). The 7 ± 2 figure is about memory span, not a menu rule.

questions.stem: You tap Save and nothing visibly changes, so you are unsure it worked. Which gulf is this?
questions.explanation: The gulf of evaluation is the gap between the system's state and your ability to tell what happened; missing feedback widens it (Slide 6).
questions.hint: Is the problem doing the action, or knowing what it did?
